content_html:
From Curiosity to Question

Every statistical investigation begins with a question someone wants to answer. A teacher wonders whether students who sleep longer perform better in tests. A public health team asks whether exercise frequency is linked to reported wellbeing. A market researcher wants to know whether younger shoppers spend more online than older ones. In each case, the curiosity is real — but curiosity alone is not enough. Statistics demands that you turn your question into something testable.

A hypothesis is a precise, testable statement — not a vague hunch. Compare these two versions of the same idea:

  • Vague question: “Do students who sleep more do better?”
  • Testable hypothesis: “Students who sleep eight or more hours per night will score higher on a memory test than students who sleep fewer than eight hours.”

The second version names the variables, states a direction, and makes clear what data you would need to collect. That precision matters because your entire investigation — what data to gather, how to sample, which statistical tools to use, and how to judge whether your results support or refute your prediction — flows from the hypothesis you write at the start.

Key Fact

A testable hypothesis names the variables involved, states a predicted relationship or difference, and can be supported or refuted through data. The specification does not require formal null-hypothesis notation — a clearly worded statement is sufficient.

Why Hypotheses Can Only Be Tested Through Data

It is tempting to think that a well-reasoned argument can “prove” a hypothesis. Statistics says no. You can believe something is true for entirely logical reasons and still be wrong when the data is collected. A hypothesis can only be tested through the appropriate collection and analysis of data — this is a core principle of the specification. Opinion, intuition, and personal experience are starting points for forming a hypothesis, not evidence for evaluating one.

This is why the design of an investigation matters so much. If your data collection is flawed — biased sample, poorly worded questions, or measurement error — then your conclusion, however confidently stated, rests on shaky foundations.

Investigation Constraints

Real investigations face practical limits. The specification lists five main types of constraint you should be able to discuss: time constraints, cost constraints, ethical issues, confidentiality concerns, and convenience.

Time: A survey conducted over one week gives a very different result from one run over a full year. If you are studying seasonal behaviour — ice cream sales, flu cases, holiday bookings — and your budget only allows one month of data collection, your results may not reflect the full picture.

Cost: A large random sample is statistically ideal but expensive. Interviewing participants in person is richer than an online questionnaire but far costlier. Many investigators compromise on sample size or method because of limited funds, and this affects the conclusions they can draw.

Ethical issues: Investigations involving human participants must not cause harm, distress, or embarrassment. Researching sensitive topics — mental health, financial hardship, relationship difficulties — requires careful handling. Participants must give their consent, and the researcher must decide whether the benefit of the knowledge outweighs any risk of harm.

Confidentiality: Data collected about individuals must be protected. If people fear that their personal information will be shared or used against them, they may refuse to participate or give dishonest answers. Guaranteeing anonymity — not attaching names to responses — typically improves both response rates and honesty.

Convenience: Sometimes the ideal population is simply not accessible. A researcher wanting to survey a random sample of all UK secondary school students faces enormous logistical challenges. Convenience shapes who can realistically be included.

A research question asks something open-ended: “Is there a relationship between screen time and sleep quality?” That is a useful starting point, but it is not a hypothesis.

A hypothesis makes a specific, directional prediction: “Students who spend more than three hours on screens per evening will report fewer hours of sleep than students who spend less than one hour on screens.” Now you know exactly what to measure, how to group participants, and what a supporting result would look like.

In the exam, if a question asks you to “write a hypothesis” and you write a question instead, you will lose marks. Make sure your answer is a statement, not a question.

Proactive Strategies: Planning for Problems

Good investigators do not just hope that problems will not arise — they plan for them. The specification expects you to know what kinds of problems can occur during an enquiry and how to mitigate them before they happen. Three common challenges are: difficulty identifying the population, non-response, and unexpected outcomes.

Identifying the population: For some investigations, the population is easy to define — all Year 11 students in a school, for example. For others, the boundary is blurry. If you want to study “regular gym users”, what counts as regular? Once per week? Five times per week? Defining the population clearly before you begin prevents disputes about who should have been included later.

Non-response: If a large proportion of people choose not to respond to your questionnaire, the results may be biased. Those who respond might systematically differ from those who do not. For example, people with strong opinions tend to respond at higher rates than those with moderate views. Strategies to reduce non-response include: keeping questionnaires short, offering an incentive, and following up with reminders.

Unexpected outcomes: Real data surprises you. A value that seems impossibly large might be a genuine outlier, a data entry error, or evidence that your hypothesis needs refinement. A good investigator builds in a review stage rather than assuming everything will go to plan.

Key Fact

Proactive strategies — such as piloting the questionnaire, offering anonymity, defining the population precisely, and building in a follow-up for non-responders — reduce the risk that problems discovered later will invalidate the entire investigation.

A student wants to test whether students who travel more than 30 minutes to school are more likely to arrive late than those who travel fewer than 30 minutes.

Hypothesis: “Students with a commute of more than 30 minutes will have a higher rate of late arrivals than students with a commute of fewer than 30 minutes.”

Constraints identified:

  • Time — data collection limited to one half-term; seasonal effects (e.g. winter delays) not captured.
  • Ethical — lateness data is sensitive; consent needed from school and parents for under-16s.
  • Non-response — some students may not return the travel-time form; a follow-up reminder planned.

Why Classifying Data Matters

Before you can choose a graph, a formula, or a statistical test, you need to know what type of data you have. A bar chart is right for some data but completely wrong for others. The mean makes sense for some measurements but is meaningless for others. Every decision in the rest of your investigation flows from the type of data you collected. Getting this classification right at the start prevents wasted effort later.

Quantitative and Qualitative Data

Quantitative data is data that takes numerical values. Height in centimetres, temperature in degrees, number of goals scored — all of these are quantitative because you can do arithmetic with them. Calculating the mean height or the total goals scored is meaningful.

Qualitative data describes qualities or categories. Eye colour, favourite genre of music, a person’s opinion expressed in their own words — these are qualitative. You cannot calculate a meaningful mean eye colour. Qualitative data is often ‘words’ rather than numbers, though it can be coded into numbers (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree) — but even then, the codes are labels, not measurements.

Key Fact

The key test: can you do meaningful arithmetic with the values? If yes, the data is quantitative. If no (e.g. averaging “nationalities” makes no sense), it is qualitative.

Categorical and Ordinal Data

Within qualitative data, two further types matter. Categorical data falls into groups with no natural ordering. Blood group (A, B, AB, O), country of birth, and make of car are categorical — there is no sensible way to say that blood group B comes ‘after’ blood group A.

Ordinal data can be ordered or ranked, but the gaps between positions are not equal. Placing first, second, or third in a race is ordinal — you know the order, but ‘first is better than second’ does not tell you by how much. Survey responses such as “poor / fair / good / excellent” are ordinal: the order is clear, but the step from ‘poor’ to ‘fair’ is not necessarily the same size as the step from ‘good’ to ‘excellent’.

Discrete and Continuous Data

Within quantitative data, two further types are essential. Discrete data can only take specific, separate values. The number of students in a class is discrete: you can have 28 or 29 students, but not 28.4. The number of goals in a match is discrete.

Continuous data can take any value within a range. Height, weight, temperature, and time are all continuous — a student’s height could theoretically be 163.47 cm. In practice, measurement tools limit the precision, but the underlying characteristic is continuous.

Why does this distinction matter? Discrete data is usually represented with bar charts and pictograms (with gaps between bars). Continuous data is represented with histograms (no gaps), or can be grouped into class intervals. You should choose the representation that matches the data type, not the one that looks nicest.

Students often argue about shoe size. In the UK, shoe sizes come in specific values (6, 6.5, 7, 7.5, ...) — there is no UK size 7.3. That makes shoe size discrete, even though it is a numerical measurement.

Contrast this with foot length in centimetres. That is continuous — a foot could be 26.2 cm or 26.25 cm. The key question is whether the measuring system has genuine gaps between values, or whether it is just rounding a continuous thing. Shoe sizes are a labelling convention, so they are discrete. Foot lengths are continuous.

Ungrouped and Grouped Data

Data can also be described as ungrouped (individual values listed separately) or grouped (values collected into class intervals). Grouping is useful when a dataset is large and spread over a wide range — it makes patterns easier to see. However, grouping loses precision: once data is grouped, you can only estimate the mean, not calculate it exactly.

When creating class intervals, check that they do not overlap and that they cover the full range of the data. The choice of class width affects how clearly the distribution is visible: too many narrow classes and the pattern is obscured by noise; too few wide classes and important detail is lost.

Explanatory and Response Variables

When an investigation explores whether one thing influences another, statisticians distinguish between two types of variable. The explanatory variable (also called the independent variable) is the one the researcher believes causes or predicts changes. The response variable (also called the dependent variable) is the outcome being measured.

Example: if you investigate whether daily revision time influences exam score, then revision time is the explanatory variable and exam score is the response variable. Plotting on a scatter graph, convention places the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis and the response variable on the vertical axis.

Key Fact

The explanatory variable goes on the horizontal (x) axis. The response variable goes on the vertical (y) axis. A memory cue: you explain how x causes changes in y.

Bivariate Data

Bivariate data is data where two measurements are taken on each individual. When you record both a student’s revision hours and their exam score, you have bivariate data — one pair of values per student. Bivariate data is used to investigate relationships: is there a correlation? Does the explanatory variable predict the response variable?

Multivariate Data (Higher)

Multivariate data is data where three or more variables are recorded for each individual. A researcher studying student performance might record revision hours, sleep duration, and exam score for each student — that is multivariate. Multivariate datasets are more realistic than bivariate ones, because real-world outcomes rarely have just a single influence.

The challenge with multivariate data is distinguishing the effect of one variable from the effects of others. If students who revise more also sleep more, it becomes difficult to say whether the exam improvement is due to revision, sleep, or both. This is why large data sets and statistical controls matter in real research.

Sometimes a questionnaire produces too many small categories. If ten students rate their commute as “less than 5 minutes”, thirty as “5–10 minutes”, and two as “50–60 minutes”, the very small categories make charts hard to read and comparisons unreliable.

Merging categories — such as combining “less than 5 minutes” and “5–10 minutes” into “up to 10 minutes” — can make the data more useful. The trade-off is that you lose detail. A good class interval choice balances readability with preserving the shape of the distribution.

Where Does Data Come From?

Every statistical investigation needs data — but that data has to come from somewhere. The two fundamental categories are primary data and secondary data. Understanding the difference between them — and knowing the advantages and limitations of each — is essential when planning an investigation and when evaluating someone else’s research.

Primary Data

Primary data is collected first-hand, specifically for your investigation. The main methods include:

  • Experimental: The researcher controls conditions to test a cause-and-effect relationship. A laboratory experiment removes external influences (high level of control). A field experiment takes place in a natural setting, which improves realism but reduces control. A natural experiment observes what happens when conditions change for non-research reasons — for example, observing the effect of a new bus route on school attendance rates.
  • Simulation: Uses models (often computer-based) to generate data when real-world collection is impossible or unethical — for example, simulating traffic patterns or the spread of an infectious disease.
  • Questionnaire: A set of written questions completed by participants. Cheap and scalable, but dependent on honest responses.
  • Observation: Watching and recording behaviour directly. Can capture what people actually do rather than what they say they do, but observer presence can influence behaviour.

Primary data has a major advantage: it is collected specifically for your purpose, so it should measure exactly what you need. The disadvantage is that it takes time and resources to collect.

Secondary Data

Secondary data already exists. Sources include published statistical databases, government censuses, academic studies, media reports, and reference publications. In the UK, organisations such as the Office for National Statistics (ONS), NHS Digital, the Met Office, and the Department for Education all publish large, high-quality datasets that researchers can use without collecting any data themselves.

The advantages of secondary data are significant: it is fast to access, often covers large populations, and may span decades of historical records that no individual researcher could replicate. The ONS Census, for example, covers the entire UK population at ten-year intervals — a dataset of that scale is simply not achievable through primary collection for most researchers.

However, secondary data has limitations. It was collected for a different purpose, so it may not measure exactly what you need. Variable definitions may differ — what counts as “unemployed” changed in UK statistics several times between the 1970s and 1990s, making long-run comparisons tricky. You also need to acknowledge the source of any secondary data you use, as the specification requires.

Key Fact

Secondary data: advantages — fast to access, large sample sizes, historical depth. Limitations — may not measure exactly what you need, variable definitions may have changed, source must be acknowledged and its quality assessed.

Census vs Sample

A census collects data from every member of the population. The UK Census, conducted every ten years, aims to record information about every household. A census gives complete data with no sampling error, but it is expensive, time-consuming, and in some cases impossible (not every person can be reached).

In contrast, sampling involves collecting data from a carefully chosen subset. Most practical investigations use samples. The challenge is making the sample representative enough that conclusions about the population are valid.

Reliability and Validity

These two words are used precisely in statistics and are often confused. Reliability is about consistency: does the measurement give the same result every time you use it? Validity is about accuracy of purpose: does the measurement capture the thing you actually want to know about?

A useful way to see the difference: imagine a bathroom scale that always reads 3 kg too heavy. It is reliable — it gives a consistent reading every time — but it is not valid for measuring your true weight. Conversely, asking students “How healthy do you feel?” on a scale of 1–10 might produce variable answers from the same student on different days (poor reliability) and may not accurately capture their clinical health status (poor validity).

Students frequently write “the data is reliable and valid” as if the two words mean the same thing, or they use one when they mean the other. In the exam, using these terms imprecisely will cost marks.

If a question asks about reliability, focus on: would repeated measurements give the same result? If it asks about validity, focus on: does the measurement actually capture what you want to measure? A questionnaire asking about income to proxy for social class is valid if income correlates well with social class — but only reliable if the same person answers the same question consistently across administrations.

Bias and Sensitivity

Bias is a systematic error — it pushes results in one direction rather than producing random noise. Bias can arise from: the way a sample is selected (sampling bias), the way questions are worded (response bias), or the sensitivity of the topic being researched.

Sensitive topics — income, health, political views, personal relationships — are particularly prone to response bias. People may give socially desirable answers rather than honest ones, or they may refuse to answer at all (non-response bias). When the people who refuse to answer share a characteristic relevant to the investigation, this creates a systematic distortion in the results.

Level of Control and Minimising Data Distortion (Higher)

In a controlled experiment, the researcher manipulates one variable (the explanatory variable) and keeps all others constant, so that any change in the response variable can be attributed to the manipulation. The level of control refers to how completely the investigator can hold other variables constant.

High control (laboratory experiments) makes causation easier to claim but may reduce ecological validity — the results may not apply to real-world settings. Low control (natural experiments, observational studies) reflects real-world conditions better but makes it harder to isolate cause and effect because other variables are free to vary.

Extraneous variables — variables that influence the response variable but are not the focus of the investigation — must be identified and managed. Techniques include controlling them directly (holding them constant across all participants), including a control group (a group that receives no treatment, against which the experimental group is compared), and randomisation (randomly assigning participants to groups so that extraneous variables are spread evenly).

Key Fact

Reliability = consistency across repeated measurements. Validity = the measurement captures what it is supposed to measure. A data source can be one without the other.

The specification explicitly states that secondary data sources should be acknowledged. In practice, this means recording where the data came from, when it was collected or published, and who collected it. This matters for two reasons.

First, it allows the reader to check the original source and assess its quality. A statistic from a government body such as the ONS is more likely to be reliable than one from a company’s own press release. Second, without acknowledgement, using someone else’s data without credit is a form of academic misconduct. In professional statistical work and in your investigation write-up, always note the source.

Why Sampling?

A population is everyone or everything the investigation concerns. But collecting data from every member of a population is often impractical — too expensive, too time-consuming, or simply impossible. Instead, a researcher selects a sample: a manageable subset from which conclusions about the whole population can be drawn.

The quality of those conclusions depends critically on how the sample is selected. A badly chosen sample — one that over-represents some groups and under-represents others — produces biased results. No amount of clever analysis can fix a biased sample. This is why choosing the right sampling method is one of the most important decisions in the planning stage of any investigation.

Before sampling can begin, you need a sample frame: a complete list of everyone in the population. For a school survey, the sample frame might be the roll of all registered students. For a national survey, a sample frame might be the electoral register or postcode address file. The sample frame may not include every member of the population — some individuals are always missed — and this itself can be a source of bias.

Methods That Rely on Judgement or Opportunity

Judgement sampling (also called purposive sampling) is where the researcher deliberately chooses participants they believe are typical. It is fast and avoids obvious outliers, but the researcher’s judgement introduces subjectivity and potential bias. If the researcher’s beliefs about the population are wrong, the sample will be wrong in a systematic way.

Opportunity sampling (also called convenience sampling) means selecting whoever is available. Surveying people who happen to be walking past at a particular time, or asking friends and classmates, are examples. It is the cheapest and fastest method, but it is highly susceptible to bias: the people who are available may systematically differ from the wider population in ways that affect the results.

A sample obtained by opportunity or judgement is not automatically worthless. If you are investigating an exploratory question — trying to identify variables worth studying in more depth — a convenient sample gives a quick first look. In early-stage research, speed can outweigh the need for perfect representativeness.

However, any conclusions drawn from such samples must be clearly caveated: they may not apply to the wider population. The examiner will expect you to state this limitation when evaluating an investigation that used judgement or opportunity sampling.

Random Sampling

In a simple random sample, every member of the population has an equal chance of being included, and selections are made using a genuinely random process. This is the gold standard for avoiding systematic bias: no group is systematically favoured or excluded.

Random selection can be achieved using various techniques, including: assigning numbers to all members of the sample frame and using a random number generator, shuffling a pack of cards, or rolling dice. The specification notes these methods but is explicit: you will not be asked to derive a sample using these techniques in the exam — understanding the principle is what matters.

Systematic Sampling

Systematic sampling selects every ‘k’th member of the sample frame after a random start. For example, to select 20 from a list of 200 people, you calculate k = 200 ÷ 20 = 10, choose a random starting point between 1 and 10, then select every 10th person after that.

Systematic sampling is easier to implement than simple random sampling for large populations, and it spreads the sample evenly across the list. However, it can introduce a hidden pattern if the sample frame itself has a regular structure. If a list alternates male/female and you sample every other entry, you might end up with an all-male or all-female sample.

Key Fact

Systematic sampling steps: (1) calculate the sampling interval k = population size ÷ sample size; (2) choose a random start between 1 and k; (3) select every k-th member after that starting point.

Stratification: Not a Sampling Method

This is one of the most commonly misunderstood ideas in the specification. Stratification is a process that happens before sampling — it is not itself a method of sampling. The specification is explicit: stratification is not a method of sampling but a method which may be used before sampling takes place.

Here is how stratification works: first, you divide the population into meaningful subgroups called strata (singular: stratum) based on a characteristic relevant to the investigation. Then, you select participants from each stratum separately, using a random method, in proportion to the size of each stratum in the population.

Example: a school has 300 students: 120 in Year 10 and 180 in Year 11. You want a sample of 50. If you stratify by year group: Year 10 contributes ​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​120/300 × 50 = 20 students; Year 11 contributes 180/300 × 50 = 30 students. Within each stratum, you then select randomly. This ensures the sample reflects the year-group balance of the school.

Key Fact

Stratification divides the population into subgroups BEFORE sampling. The actual sampling method used within each stratum is then random sampling. Calling stratification a “sampling method” is a common error that costs marks.

Quota Sampling (Higher)

Quota sampling looks similar to stratification on the surface: you set a target for each subgroup. But there is a crucial difference. In stratified random sampling, participants within each stratum are chosen randomly. In quota sampling, the researcher fills each quota using whoever is available — there is no random selection within the quota. A market researcher might be told to interview 30 women aged 18–25 and 30 women aged 26–40, but they then choose those 60 participants by opportunity — approaching people in a shopping centre until the quotas are met.

Quota sampling is fast and proportional to the population structure, which is why commercial market research firms often use it. However, because selection within each quota is not random, it is susceptible to the same biases as opportunity sampling. The people a researcher approaches in a shopping centre on a weekday morning systematically differ from those who are at work.

Every sampling method trades off between cost/speed and bias risk. Understanding these trade-offs is what the specification is really testing:

  • Opportunity: Fast, cheap, highly biased. Useful only for pilot/exploratory work.
  • Judgement: Fast, avoids obvious outliers, still subjective. Researcher’s assumptions must be sound.
  • Random: Unbiased in expectation, but requires a complete sample frame and may still miss subgroups by chance in small samples.
  • Systematic: Practical for large populations; watch for hidden patterns in the list.
  • Stratification then random: Best for populations with important subgroups — guarantees proportional representation.

lesson_title: Questionnaires, Pilot Studies and Cleaning Data
content_html:
Designing a Good Questionnaire

A questionnaire is only as good as the questions it contains. Even with a perfect sample, a poorly designed questionnaire will produce data that is biased, incomplete, or simply not measuring what you intended. The specification identifies several key features to consider: leading questions, avoiding biased sources, the choice of open or closed questions, interview technique, and time factors.

Leading Questions

A leading question nudges the respondent towards a particular answer. Consider these two versions:

  • Leading: “Don’t you agree that students should do at least one hour of exercise a day?”
  • Neutral: “How many hours of exercise do you do on a typical day?”

The first version makes it socially awkward to disagree. Respondents who exercise very little may inflate their answers to avoid seeming lazy. The second makes no assumption. Always ask: does this question imply there is a right or preferred answer? If yes, rewrite it.

Which of these is leading? Think before reading on.

  • 1. “How often do you eat unhealthy food?” — Leading. The word “unhealthy” primes the respondent to under-report.
  • 2. “What type of food do you eat most often?” — Not leading. No assumption is built in.
  • 3. “Most young people spend too much time on their phones. How many hours do you spend on your phone per day?” — Leading. The preamble sets an expectation that shapes the answer.

Open and Closed Questions

Open questions invite free-text answers. The response might be detailed and revealing, but every answer is different — comparing many different written opinions requires careful judgement rather than straightforward statistical analysis.

Closed questions provide fixed options. The data is straightforward to count and compare. Always check that closed-question options are exhaustive (they cover all possible answers) and mutually exclusive (no answer fits more than one option).

Key Fact

Open questions: rich detail but hard to analyse statistically. Closed questions: easy to count and compare but may not capture every possible view. Good questionnaires often use both types.

Interview Technique and Time Factors

The way an interview is conducted can affect responses. Face-to-face interviews allow clarification of confusing questions, but the interviewer’s presence can cause socially desirable answers. Telephone or online questionnaires offer more anonymity, which may encourage more honest responses on sensitive topics, though response rates are often lower.

Time factors matter too. Asking about sleep habits on a Monday (after a weekend) will produce different answers from asking mid-week. Seasonal effects can skew data about outdoor activities, mental wellbeing, or energy consumption. A good questionnaire design considers when the questions will be asked and whether timing could bias the results.

Pilot Studies

A pilot study is a small-scale practice run — you administer the questionnaire to a small group before the main data collection. It serves several purposes:

  • Identifying ambiguous or unclear questions that respondents interpret differently.
  • Checking that response categories are exhaustive and mutually exclusive.
  • Estimating how long the questionnaire takes, so respondents can be informed.
  • Revealing leading or loaded language the researcher did not notice when writing the questions.

The pilot participants are typically not included in the main investigation. After the pilot, the questionnaire is revised before real data collection begins. Skipping the pilot is a common planning mistake — it is far cheaper to fix problems before 500 responses are collected than afterwards.

Cleaning Data

Raw data is rarely perfect. Before analysis begins, the dataset must be cleaned — checked and corrected for errors and inconsistencies. The specification identifies several types of problem that require data cleaning:

Missing data: Some respondents skip questions. A missing value cannot be included in calculations — you must decide whether to exclude the incomplete response, impute a value, or note the gap and acknowledge the effect on your results.

Non-responses: The entire questionnaire is not returned. If non-respondents share a characteristic, excluding them introduces bias.

Incorrect formats: A question asking for age might receive “sixteen” (text) alongside numerical entries. Spreadsheet software cannot calculate with inconsistent formats, so these must be standardised.

Extraneous notation: Currency symbols, spaces, or units entered inconsistently (“£4500” vs “4500” vs “4,500”) will prevent calculations. These must be removed or standardised before analysis.

Key Fact

Three main data cleaning problems: (1) missing data — blank cells where responses were skipped; (2) incorrect formats — inconsistent data entry; (3) extraneous notation — symbols or punctuation that prevent calculation.

Spotting Errors Using Row and Column Totals

One practical cleaning technique is to check whether values in a row or column are internally consistent. If the row total for a group is 45 but the three individual entries sum to 50, one entry is wrong. The specification notes that students may be asked to use row or column totals to identify a wrongly recorded value.

A worked example: a table records the number of books read by students in three year groups over two terms. If Year 9’s Term 1 column total is 120 but the individual class entries are 42, 38, and 45 (summing to 125), one of these three entries has been incorrectly recorded and needs investigating.

Control Groups and Extraneous Variables (Higher)

When an investigation compares two groups — for example, students who received a new study intervention versus those who did not — the group that does not receive the treatment is the control group. Without a control group, you cannot know whether any improvement is due to the intervention or would have happened anyway.

Extraneous variables — factors that could influence the outcome but are not the variable being tested — must be identified and held constant where possible. For example, if testing whether music helps concentration, room temperature and time of day are extraneous variables that should be kept the same across both groups.

An incomplete response is one where a participant returns the questionnaire but leaves some questions blank — perhaps because a question was unclear or felt too personal. A non-response is where the questionnaire is not returned at all.

Both create gaps in the data. Incomplete responses might be rescued for the questions that were answered, whereas non-responses produce no usable data. In both cases, if those affected share a characteristic, the results are biased.

unit_name: Interpreting Results & The Statistical Enquiry Cycle
lesson_title: Correlation, Causation and the Vocabulary of Association
content_html:
What Is Correlation?

When two variables tend to change together, we say there is a correlation between them. Correlation is about pattern, not proof. Statisticians have a precise vocabulary for describing correlations, and using the right term in the right context is one of the most reliable ways to pick up marks in interpretation questions.

Direction: Positive, Negative and Zero

Positive correlation means that as one variable increases, the other tends to increase too. Hours of revision and exam score typically show positive correlation: students who revise more tend to score higher.

Negative correlation means that as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease. Distance from the city centre and house price often show negative correlation: properties further from the centre tend to cost less (though this depends heavily on context).

Zero correlation (no correlation) means there is no consistent relationship between the two variables. The points on a scatter graph are scattered randomly with no discernible pattern.

Key Fact

The three directions: positive correlation (both variables increase together), negative correlation (one increases as the other decreases), zero correlation (no consistent pattern). The word “moderate” for correlation strength is NOT used in this specification — use strong, weak, or no correlation only.

Strength: Strong, Weak and No Correlation

The strength of a correlation describes how closely the points cluster around a straight line. The specification defines precise thresholds for strength based on the value of the correlation coefficient \(r\):

  • Strong correlation: \(|r| \geq 0.6\) (i.e. \(r \geq 0.6\) or \(r \leq -0.6\))
  • Weak correlation: \(0.2 \leq |r| < 0.6\) (i.e. between 0.2 and 0.6 in magnitude)
  • No correlation: \(|r| < 0.2\) (i.e. between \(-0.2\) and \(0.2\), not including these endpoints)

These thresholds are fixed by the specification. Do not use the word “moderate” — the specification explicitly excludes this term. Do not make up your own thresholds. Use strong, weak, or no correlation as described above.

Interpolation and Extrapolation

Interpolation means using the line of best fit to estimate a value that falls within the range of the data you collected. If your data covers ages 20 to 60 and you estimate for age 35, that is interpolation. Interpolation is generally considered reliable when the correlation is strong.

Extrapolation means extending the line beyond the range of your data to estimate a value. If your data covers ages 20 to 60 and you try to estimate for age 80, that is extrapolation. Extrapolation is much less reliable — the relationship seen within the data range may not continue outside it. The line of best fit might predict a negative house price if extended far enough, which is obviously impossible.

Key Fact

Interpolation (within the data range) is generally more reliable. Extrapolation (beyond the data range) is risky because the relationship seen in the data may not continue outside it. The further you extrapolate, the less reliable the estimate.

Causation vs Association

This is the most important idea in this lesson — and one of the most commonly examined. Finding a strong correlation between two variables does NOT mean that one causes the other. The specification explicitly states: correlation does not necessarily imply causation.

Consider this: there is a strong positive correlation between ice cream sales and drowning incidents over time. Does ice cream cause drowning? No. Both variables share a common cause: hot weather. People buy more ice cream in hot weather, and more people swim in hot weather, leading to more drowning incidents. The ice cream and the drowning are both responses to the temperature — they did not cause each other.

The hidden factor that explains both variables is called a lurking variable (also called a confounding variable). The specification says you should know that there are multiple factors that may interact. Any time you see a strong correlation, a good statistician asks: “Is there a third variable that could explain this?”

This is one of the most tested misconceptions in GCSE Statistics. Students see a correlation of 0.8 and write “the increase in X causes an increase in Y.” This will cost marks.

The correct language is: “There is a strong positive correlation between X and Y. This suggests X and Y are associated, but this does not mean X causes Y. There could be a lurking variable that explains both.” Using the word “associated” rather than “causes” shows the examiner you understand the distinction.

Interpreting Spearman's Rank and Pearson's PMCC (Higher)

At Higher tier, you need to interpret calculated values of two correlation coefficients. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient measures the strength and direction of correlation between the rank orders of two variables — not the raw values. It works for any data that can be ranked, including ordinal data.

Pearson's product moment correlation coefficient (PMCC) measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables. The key distinction: Spearman's measures correlation of rank orders, whereas Pearson's measures the linear relationship itself. For a straight-line relationship between continuous variables, Pearson's is more appropriate; for ranked or ordinal data, Spearman's is preferred.

The formula for Spearman's rank will always be given in the question — you do not need to memorise it. What you do need to do is interpret the resulting value using the same thresholds above: \(|r_s| \geq 0.6\) = strong, \(0.2 \leq |r_s| < 0.6\) = weak, \(|r_s| < 0.2\) = no correlation.

A researcher finds a Spearman's rank correlation coefficient of \(-0.72\) between students' daily screen time and their reading test scores.

Step 1: Direction — the value is negative, so this is a negative correlation. As screen time increases, reading scores tend to decrease.

Step 2: Strength — \(|-0.72| = 0.72\), which is \(\geq 0.6\), so this is a strong negative correlation.

Step 3: Causation caution — this does not prove that screen time causes lower reading scores. Other factors (e.g. time available for reading, parental education) might explain both variables.

unit_name: Interpreting Results & The Statistical Enquiry Cycle
content_html:
What Is a Distribution?

When you collect a set of data, the values spread across a range. The way those values are spread — which values are common, which are rare, whether the data clusters symmetrically or leans to one side — is the distribution of the data. Reading the shape of a distribution is a core interpretation skill: it tells you whether the data is symmetric, skewed, or has unusual values at the extremes.

Symmetrical Distributions

A symmetrical distribution is balanced — the left and right sides are roughly mirror images of each other. In a perfectly symmetrical distribution, the mean, median, and mode are all equal and sit at the centre. A classic symmetrical shape is the bell curve, which you will encounter later in this lesson when looking at the Normal distribution.

Positive Skew

A positively skewed distribution has a longer tail on the right. Most values cluster at the lower end of the scale, with a few unusually high values stretching the tail to the right. Because those extreme high values pull the mean upwards, the mean is greater than the median in a positively skewed distribution.

A real-world example: household income in the UK is positively skewed. Most households earn in a moderate range, but a small number of very high earners stretch the tail. The mean income is pulled upwards by these high earners, making it higher than the median. This is why the median is often a more representative average for income data.

Negative Skew

A negatively skewed distribution has a longer tail on the left. Most values cluster at the higher end of the scale, with a few unusually low values stretching the tail to the left. The mean is pulled downwards by those extreme low values, making it less than the median.

A real-world example: scores on an easy test might show negative skew. Most students score highly (the cluster is on the right), but a small number of students who struggled pull the tail to the left. The mean score would be lower than the median because of those very low scores.

Key Fact

Positive skew: tail on the right, mean > median. Negative skew: tail on the left, mean < median. A useful memory trick: the skew is named after the direction of the TAIL, not the main cluster.

Key Fact

Positive skew: tail on the right, mean > median. Negative skew: tail on the left, mean < median. Symmetrical: mean = median. Remember: the skew is named after the direction of the TAIL, not where the main cluster sits.

Commenting on Outliers

An outlier is a value that stands apart from the rest of the data — either much larger or much smaller than typical. Outliers can arise from genuine extreme values (a student who scored 100% on a test where everyone else scored between 40% and 80%), measurement errors (a data entry typo turning 160 cm into 16 cm), or a genuinely different subgroup in the data.

When commenting on outliers in exam questions, you should: (1) identify the outlier by referring to its approximate value, (2) suggest whether it might be a genuine extreme value or a possible error, and (3) comment on its effect on any averages you have calculated. An outlier pulls the mean towards it but does not affect the median.

Students often say “positive skew has most values on the positive side of the graph.” This is wrong. Positive skew is named after the direction of the TAIL, not where the main cluster sits. In a positively skewed distribution, the TAIL goes right (in the positive direction) and the CLUSTER sits at the lower end.

A quick check: if someone earned the most money in a room, are they pulling the mean income up? Yes — so income data is likely positively skewed (long right tail, even though most people cluster at lower incomes). That is positive skew.

Binomial Distribution (Higher)

A binomial distribution describes the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials, where each trial has the same probability of success. The word “binomial” will appear in your exam. The key characteristics are:

  • A fixed number of trials (e.g. flipping a coin 5 times).
  • Each trial has only two possible outcomes (success or failure).
  • The probability of success is constant across all trials.
  • The trials are independent of each other.

In your exam, the number of trials \(n\) will be no greater than 5. The distribution is symmetric when the probability of success is 0.5, and skewed when the probability is not 0.5. You do not need to use formal notation for the binomial distribution — describing its characteristics in words is sufficient.

The Normal Distribution and the 68/95 Rule (Higher)

The Normal distribution is a symmetric, bell-shaped distribution where values cluster around the mean and become progressively rarer further away. It describes many real-world characteristics: the heights of adults, birth weights, exam scores, and measurement errors all tend to follow approximately Normal distributions.

The specification requires you to know two key results about the Normal distribution:

  • Approximately 68% of the data lies within one standard deviation of the mean.
  • Approximately 95% of the data lies within two standard deviations of the mean.
  • Values more than three standard deviations from the mean are very unusual.

Action and Warning Lines in Quality Assurance (Higher)

In manufacturing and quality control, products are sampled regularly to check they meet a standard. The Normal distribution is used to set warning lines (at two standard deviations from the target) and action lines (at three standard deviations from the target). If a sample mean falls outside the action lines, the production process is stopped and investigated, because such a result would be very unusual if the process were running correctly.

Standardising Data (Higher)

To compare values from two different distributions (e.g. a student's score in Maths and their score in English, which have different means and standard deviations), you can standardise by converting each value to a z-score: $$z = rac{x - ar{x}}{s}$$ where \(x\) is the value, \( ar{x}\) is the mean, and \(s\) is the standard deviation. The formula will be given in the question. A z-score tells you how many standard deviations above or below the mean a value lies, allowing fair comparison across different scales.

The heights of a group of adults are Normally distributed with a mean of 170 cm and a standard deviation of 8 cm.

Within one standard deviation (162 cm to 178 cm): approximately 68% of adults. Within two standard deviations (154 cm to 186 cm): approximately 95% of adults. Heights above 194 cm or below 146 cm (three standard deviations away) are very unusual.

lesson_title: Time Series, Trends and Rates of Change
content_html:
What Is a Time Series?

A time series is data recorded at successive time points — monthly sales figures, quarterly unemployment rates, annual birth rates. Plotting these values against time produces a time series graph (sometimes called a line chart) that lets you see patterns that would be invisible in a table of numbers.

Trends

The trend is the overall direction a time series is heading in the long run, ignoring short-term ups and downs. A trend might be rising (e.g. average house prices in the UK over decades), falling (e.g. infant mortality rates over the last century), or roughly constant. Identifying the trend is the first step in interpreting a time series.

It is important to distinguish the trend from short-term variation. A shop’s weekly sales might spike before Christmas and dip in January, but the underlying trend over several years might be consistently rising. The trend is what you would see if you smoothed out the seasonal bumps.

Key Fact

A trend is the long-term overall direction. A seasonal pattern is a regular, repeating short-term fluctuation at the same time each year (or each cycle). Both can be present in the same time series.

Seasonal and Cyclic Trends

A seasonal trend is a regular, repeating pattern tied to the time of year. Ice cream sales peak in summer and fall in winter every year; gas and electricity consumption peaks in winter every year; retail sales peak before Christmas every year. These patterns are predictable and expected.

A cyclic trend is similar but not tied to a fixed calendar period — it represents a pattern that rises and falls over a longer, less regular time scale (such as economic business cycles that might last several years). The specification uses the term “cyclic” as well as “seasonal” and you should be able to interpret both.

When a question asks you to use a seasonal or cyclic trend to make a prediction, always say: “Based on the seasonal pattern in the data, I would expect [variable] to [rise/fall] in [period] because [reason from the pattern].” Predictions based on time series should acknowledge that the pattern may not continue indefinitely.

Rates of Change

A rate of change expresses how quickly something changes over time. Rather than just showing the raw count, a rate puts change in proportion — allowing meaningful comparison between populations of different sizes or time periods of different lengths.

The specification covers several specific rate measures used in real UK contexts. These include the birth rate (number of live births per 1,000 people per year), the death rate (number of deaths per 1,000 people per year), house price change, and unemployment rates. All rate-of-change formulae will be given in the question — you will not be asked to recall them from memory. What matters is reading the formula carefully and applying it correctly to the data given.

A larger country has more births per year than a smaller one, simply because it has more people. Comparing raw birth counts tells you little. The birth rate (births per 1,000 population) corrects for population size, allowing a fair comparison between countries or regions of different sizes.

Similarly, a rise in the number of deaths does not necessarily mean mortality is worsening — the population may have grown or aged. The death rate puts this in proportion. Always use rates when comparing populations of different sizes.

Index Numbers

Index numbers express a value relative to a chosen base period (usually set to 100). Instead of quoting actual prices or quantities, an index shows how much a value has changed from the base. If the base year has an index of 100 and a later year has an index of 115, then the value has risen by 15% from the base.

UK economists and statisticians use three important index numbers that you should know by name:

  • RPI (Retail Price Index): Measures changes in the average price of a basket of goods and services purchased by households. Published monthly by the ONS. Used for uprating certain benefits, wages, and rail fares.
  • CPI (Consumer Price Index): Similar to RPI but uses a different methodology and basket of goods. The Bank of England uses CPI as its target measure for inflation.
  • GDP (Gross Domestic Product): Measures the total economic output of a country. GDP index tracks growth or contraction of the economy over time.
Key Fact

RPI and CPI both measure price inflation, with RPI and CPI differing in methodology. GDP measures total economic output. All three are published by UK government bodies and used in policy decisions. All rate-of-change formulae are given in the exam — focus on reading and applying them, not memorising them.

Calculating Rates of Change (Higher)

At Higher tier, you will be asked to calculate rates of change from tables using a formula that is given in the question. Typical examples include: calculating a birth rate from a table of births and population figures, or calculating a percentage change in house price from year-to-year data.

The key skill is identifying the right values to substitute into the formula. Read the column headers carefully to identify which values go where. State your working clearly and give your answer in the correct units (rates are usually expressed per 1,000 or as a percentage).

Weighted Index Numbers (Higher)

A weighted index number assigns different weights to different items based on their importance in a typical household’s spending. For example, if a family spends 40% of its budget on housing and 5% on entertainment, housing gets a much larger weight in the index. A simple (unweighted) average of all price changes would understate the effect of rising housing costs on the household’s total bill.

The CPI and RPI are both weighted indices. The formula for a weighted index will be given in the question. Your task is to apply it correctly: multiply each item’s price relative by its weight, sum these products, and divide by the sum of the weights.

When asked to interpret a time series graph in the exam, work through these steps:

  • State the overall trend — is it rising, falling, or steady over the period shown?
  • Identify any seasonal pattern — is there a regular peak and trough that repeats each year or cycle?
  • Note any unusual features — a sudden spike or dip that breaks the trend; is there a plausible real-world explanation?
  • Quantify where possible — “the value rose from approximately 40 to 65 between 2010 and 2020” is better than “it went up.”

unit_name: Interpreting Results & The Statistical Enquiry Cycle
lesson_title: The Statistical Enquiry Cycle: Reviewing the Whole Investigation
content_html:
This lesson covers the general principles of the Statistical Enquiry Cycle that apply to all students. The specific investigation, data and methods your class used in your coursework or class project will be different — refer to your teacher's notes alongside this lesson.

The Statistical Enquiry Cycle

Statistics is not just a collection of techniques — it is a systematic way of answering questions about the world. The Statistical Enquiry Cycle (SEC) is the overarching framework that ties all the individual techniques together. Each of your two exam papers ends with a question that integrates all five stages of the SEC, so understanding the cycle thoroughly is essential.

The five stages are:

  • Stage 1: Initial Planning — Define a question or hypothesis to investigate. Decide what data to collect, how to collect and record it, and how to process and represent it. Justify each decision.
  • Stage 2: Data Collection — Collect the data using the chosen method (primary or secondary). Recognise constraints, acknowledge sources, and be aware of sensitivity issues.
  • Stage 3: Data Processing and Presentation — Organise and clean the data. Choose appropriate graphs and statistical measures. Use technology to automate processing where appropriate.
  • Stage 4: Interpretation of Results — Analyse diagrams and calculations. Draw conclusions that relate back to the original question or hypothesis. Make inferences or predictions and discuss reliability.
  • Stage 5: Evaluation and Review — Identify weaknesses in approach or representation. Suggest improvements. Refine the process to investigate further.
Key Fact

The five stages of the SEC: (1) Initial Planning, (2) Data Collection, (3) Data Processing and Presentation, (4) Interpretation of Results, (5) Evaluation and Review. Both exam papers end with a SEC question that tests your ability to link all five stages.

Stage 1 in Detail: Initial Planning

Good planning makes all subsequent stages easier. At Stage 1, you must define a testable hypothesis, decide what data you need (and why), choose your sampling method (and justify it), and plan how you will process the data. Decisions made at this stage affect every other stage. A vague hypothesis leads to ambiguous data; a biased sampling method undermines any conclusion.

Stage 4 in Detail: Interpretation of Results

Interpretation is where your statistics turn into meaning. You must analyse the graphs and measures you calculated, reach conclusions that relate to your original question, and discuss the reliability of your findings. Conclusions must be in context — not “the mean is higher” but “students who revised more than five hours scored higher on average, with a mean of 72% compared to 58% for those who revised fewer than two hours.”

Reliability of findings depends on several factors: the size of the sample, how representative it is, whether the data collection method was valid, and whether there are alternative explanations for the pattern seen. Always consider: could a lurking variable explain this result? Could sampling bias have inflated or deflated the finding?

Stage 5 in Detail: Evaluation and Review

Evaluation is not about listing everything that went well — it is about identifying specific weaknesses and suggesting specific improvements. The examiner wants to see that you understand why a weakness matters, not just that something could have been done differently.

The structure that scores highest in evaluation questions: (1) identify a weakness at a specific SEC stage, (2) explain why that weakness undermines the conclusion, (3) suggest a specific improvement. This three-part structure applies whether you are evaluating a fictional enquiry or your own class investigation.

The 8-mark SEC Critique question (one of the highest-mark questions in each paper) presents a fictional investigation scenario and asks you to evaluate it. The structure that scores Mastering is:

Step 1: Identify a weakness at one SEC stage (e.g. Stage 2 — Data Collection: “The investigator used opportunity sampling from one shopping centre.”)

Step 2: Explain why this weakness undermines the conclusion: “This means the sample is likely biased towards shoppers at that location, who may differ systematically in their habits from the wider population. The conclusion therefore cannot be generalised.”

Step 3: Suggest a specific improvement: “A stratified random sample drawn from a complete sample frame of the target population would reduce this bias.”

Step 4: Repeat for a second SEC stage (e.g. Stage 1 — Planning: “The hypothesis is vague and does not specify measurable variables.”)

Mastering responses identify weaknesses at TWO different SEC stages and follow the three-step structure for each. Students who describe what the investigation did rather than evaluate its limitations score Emerging or Developing only.

Target Audience and Communication

Stage 4 also involves communicating your findings clearly to a target audience. A report written for a school governor has different requirements from one written for a science journal. The specification expects you to consider: is the level of technical language appropriate? Are the graphs and tables clearly labelled? Do the conclusions use plain, accessible language?

Good communication means presenting conclusions clearly and concisely, using appropriate visualisations, and not overloading the reader with unnecessary technical detail. Poor communication — even when the statistics are correct — means the findings fail to reach the people who need to act on them.

Sample Size, Reliability and Replication

The specification makes an important point about sample size: replication — the ability of another researcher to reach a similar conclusion by repeating the study — is more likely when the sample is large and representative. A finding based on 10 participants is much less replicable than one based on 1,000.

A larger sample reduces the impact of random variation on the results. In a very small sample, one or two unusual respondents can dominate the findings. In a larger sample, their influence is diluted. This is why increasing sample size is one of the most commonly recommended improvements in evaluation questions.

Distribution of Sample Means (Higher)

When you take many different samples from the same population and calculate the mean of each, those sample means form their own distribution. The specification requires you to know, at an intuitive level, that a set of sample means is more closely distributed (less spread out) than the individual values from the same population. This means the mean of any given sample is a better estimate of the population mean than any single individual value from the population would be.

Why? Individual values in a population are spread widely by natural variability. But when you take a mean of several values, the high values and low values in the sample tend to cancel each other out, pulling the sample mean back towards the centre. The larger the sample, the more this cancellation effect reduces the spread of sample means.

You do not need to use any formal notation for this idea — a clear verbal explanation in context is sufficient. If asked in an exam: “The sample means form a tighter distribution than the individual values because extreme values within each sample cancel out when averaged.”

The most common reason for losing marks in SEC evaluation questions is describing rather than evaluating. Describing says: “The investigator used opportunity sampling.” Evaluating says: “The use of opportunity sampling means the sample over-represents people who visit shopping centres, which may differ from the wider population in their habits — so the conclusions cannot be generalised.”

Every evaluation point needs three parts: (1) what the weakness is, (2) why it matters for the conclusion, (3) what specific change would fix it. Missing any of these parts limits your mark to Developing at best.

Key Fact

Evaluation structure for full marks: (1) identify the weakness at a named SEC stage, (2) explain why it undermines the conclusion, (3) suggest a specific, actionable improvement. Use this structure for both weaknesses in an 8-mark question.
